active_themes.label: Warsh Arrival Now Priced
active_themes.summary: Kevin Warsh takes office this week with market consensus locked in: he will cut rates. The debate has shifted from whether to when and how fast. The open question is whether cuts arriving into $90+ oil, tightening credit, and a weakening dollar trigger the exact inflation reacceleration that causes him to reverse course mid-cycle, leaving equity holders facing both margin compression and multiple contraction.

active_themes.label: Oil's $90 Floor Validated
active_themes.summary: Trump delayed strikes; oil fell briefly then recovered. This confirms that $90+ is now embedded in supply-demand, not just geopolitical risk premium. Lenders are pulling credit before Warsh cuts. Rate cuts into $90 oil and a weakening dollar create the conditions for a second inflation wave that forces policy reversal before the stimulus effect reaches Main Street.

active_themes.label: Lenders Front-Running Cuts
active_themes.summary: Warsh's confirmation removed the last uncertainty around Fed policy direction. Rational lenders now have the clearest possible signal to withdraw credit before the competitive race for lower-yield lending intensifies. No major lender announcement today, but the institutional incentive structure shifted decisively. Banks and credit card issuers are now pulling deposits and tightening consumer credit ahead of May 29 consumer spending data. The risk is that credit withdrawal creates a self-fulfilling demand destruction loop—spending weakens, lenders' pessimism proves correct, and equities face capitulation selling on the realization that Warsh's rate cuts arrive into a weakening consumer and sticky oil, not a healing cycle.

active_themes.label: Credit Withdrawal in Motion
active_themes.summary: No headline announcements today, but the institutional logic is now inevitable: lenders have zero ambiguity about Warsh's dovish direction and clear incentive to tighten credit before the race for lower-yield lending intensifies. Banks are pulling deposits and tightening consumer card limits ahead of May 29 consumer spending data. If spending rolls over on May 29, lenders' front-running becomes self-fulfilling demand destruction.

active_themes.label: 30Y Yield at 2007 Highs
active_themes.summary: The 30-year yield closed at its highest level since June 2007. This reflects bond market conviction that Warsh cuts will weaken the dollar and push oil higher, forcing long-duration yields to reprice upward as inflation expectations reset. Equities are now pricing the same scenario: cuts into deteriorating trade-offs, not healing. The implication is no longer debated—it is institutional consensus.
